tier_reason: The JOSS paper is peer-reviewed: review issue openjournals/joss-reviews#6099 is labelled accepted/published, and a search result gives DOI 10.21105/joss.06099. Its plots show faer beating OpenBLAS on QR and mid-size eigendecomposition. No benchmark code, Rust version or flags are given, so it cannot be A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: JOSS paper text: 'State of the art algorithms are used for each decomposition, allowing performance that matches or even surpasses other low level libraries such as OpenBLAS, LAPACK, and Eigen.' Approximate readings from the paper's linked PDF plots (derived from page data; i5-11400, 12 threads, f64, n^3/s): QR at n=10^4 is about 1.48e11 for faer vs about 0.5e11 for OpenBLAS (~3x) and about 0.29e11 for Eigen, but below MKL (~1.57e11). Matmul is on par with OpenBLAS, MKL and BLIS at large n (~1.3e11) and ahead of OpenBLAS at some mid sizes (~100-300). Eigendecomposition is ahead of OpenBLAS around n=1000 (~2.2e9 vs ~1.2e9) but behind OpenBLAS, BLIS and MKL at n=10^4 (~2.9e9 vs ~3.7e9, ~4.0e9 and ~4.6e9). The f128 plots compare only against Eigen; there faer is several times faster at large n (about 3x on matmul, about 10x on QR).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated beyond 'Eigen is compiled with the -fopenmp flag'. The paper gives no Rust toolchain, faer version, optimization flags or BLAS/MKL versions.
corrections.caveats: The paper's numbers exist only as plots: PDFs attached to the GitHub repo in 2023, while the reviewed release was faer v0.24.4, so the plots predate current code. The readings above are approximate. faer is slower than MKL on QR and eigendecomposition and level with it on matmul, and it loses to OpenBLAS and BLIS on large eigendecompositions. The paper links no benchmark code and gives no Rust toolchain, flags or library versions. JOSS reviews software rather than benchmark methodology, and the benchmarks are first-party. The project's benchmark page (faer.veganb.tw/benchmarks/) and joss.theoj.org were unreachable from this container. The GitHub repository is a mirror; development moved to codeberg.org/sarah-quinones/faer. The library is Rust; a C API is only planned.

notes: The quote is verbatim in paper.md. I rendered the three linked PDF plots (matmul, QR, EVD) and read them: the win over OpenBLAS is real for QR and mid-size EVD, faer is level on matmul and loses to MKL. I removed the record's unopened 'author concedes' statement from caveats. The page confirms MIT, 2.6k stars and the last commit on 2026-09-04.

tier_reason: Upgraded from B. The full benchmark code is printed on the page and lives in SciMLBenchmarks.jl (benchmarks/LinearSolve/LUFactorization.jmd). The page states the compiler (official Julia 1.12.7, LLVM 18.1.7, znver2, default JIT optimization), the complete package manifest (RecursiveFactorization v0.2.26, OpenBLAS_jll 0.3.29, MKL_jll 2025.2.0) and the CPU (AMD EPYC 7502), which meets A. The numbers are plot readings only.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'For small to medium sized matrices, it is beneficial to use RecursiveFactorization over OpenBLAS'. The SciMLBenchmarks page has only a plot (N = 4..500). Read off it (approximate, derived from page data), RFLUFactorization reaches about 33 GFLOPs at N=500, against about 18 for OpenBLAS LUFactorization and about 23 for MKLLUFactorization. It is roughly 2x OpenBLAS around N=100-250 (about 19-21 vs 10-11 near N=200-240). MKL's noisy curve spikes above RF at a few sizes (about 34 vs about 29 near N=440).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.12.7 official release (LLVM 18.1.7 ORCJIT, znver2), default JIT optimization, JULIA_NUM_THREADS=auto (128 threads on 128 virtual cores). LinearSolve v5.5.0, RecursiveFactorization v0.2.26, OpenBLAS_jll 0.3.29, MKL_jll 2025.2.0. BenchmarkTools @belapsed with 0.5 s per sample. BLAS.set_num_threads(min(VectorizationBase.num_cores(), Threads.nthreads())); the page does not print the resulting count.
corrections.caveats: The numbers exist only as a plot, so the values above are approximate. The suite is run by the SciML organization, whose maintainers also maintain this package (recent commits come from SciML), so it is not independent. BLAS threads were set to min(num_cores, nthreads) on a 128-virtual-core EPYC runner for matrices of at most 500x500. Threading overhead in OpenBLAS and MKL may therefore inflate the gap, and the page says neither how many BLAS threads resulted nor how many threads RFLU used. MKL needed the LoadMKL_JLL preference to run on this AMD EPYC and may not use its fastest code paths there. Only N <= 500 is measured, matching the README's own 'small to medium' claim. The README's embedded plot is an older image. I did not open docs.sciml.ai; I used the raw markdown and figure from SciMLBenchmarksOutput.

notes: The raw benchmark markdown and figure LUFactorization_1_1.png were opened, and the record's plot readings are consistent with them. The page confirms MIT (LICENSE.md), 83 stars and the last commit on 2026-08-09. I left the record's '128 threads' claim out: the page does not show the value that num_cores() returned.

tier_reason: The README gives first-party numbers on an Apple M2 Max, and the benchmark code is public (benchmarks/bench_dgemm.c, bench_paper.c) with -O3 flags in the Makefile. No compiler or Xcode version is stated, and the quoted DGEMM rows do not appear in the committed results, so the tier is C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: clang: -Wall -Wextra -O3 -std=c11 for C and -O3 -fobjc-arc for the Objective-C++ Metal sources (Makefile). The compiler and Xcode version are not stated; the README requires an Xcode 16+ SDK for MTLMathModeSafe.
corrections.caveats: The numbers are first-party from one machine (M2 Max), with no compiler version. The README's DGEMM rows (552 vs 468 GFLOP/s at 2048^2, 643 vs 566 at 4096^2) are not in the committed results. benchmarks/results/2026-04-23-5cfcd52/bench_paper.csv shows 656 vs 560 (1.17x) and 672 vs 604 (1.11x). The README headline says 618 GFLOP/s, and its prior-art table lists Accelerate at 536. benchmarks/bench_dgemm.c times only ab_dgemm on matrices already uploaded to the GPU, so FP64-to-double-float conversion, upload and download fall outside the timed loop, while the Accelerate loop is timed whole. Only 5 iterations are run at N >= 2048, and Accelerate's thread count is left at its default. Per the repo's own results file, the GPU path loses to Accelerate below about N=1024-1536 (0.11x at 256, 0.95x at 1024) and on the Quantum ESPRESSO-like tall-skinny ZGEMM shapes (0.38-0.88x); ZHERK runs at 0.07-0.56x. The 22% Quantum ESPRESSO wall-time win is against 6-thread OpenBLAS, not Accelerate, and the Fortran bridge routes calls under 100M FLOPs to OpenBLAS/Accelerate. Double-float arithmetic gives a ~48-bit mantissa, not IEEE FP64. The normwise error is ~1e-14, but the same results file reports a maximum per-element relative error of up to 2.3e-7 (4096x150, K=150), and 'bit-identical energy' means agreement to the 8 printed decimals of the Ry energy. The project is Apple-GPU only (Metal) and has 3 stars.

notes: The record's numbers match the README table. The main shortcomings are methodological. GPU timings exclude data conversion and transfer. The README numbers differ from the committed results run. The repo's own results show the GPU losing to Accelerate on the QE-shaped ZGEMM calls behind the 22% application claim. The page confirms MIT, 3 stars and the last commit on 2026-04-25.
